Each issue says which version of these rules it follows. Every change is listed [at the end of this page](#changes). A new dataset or source is added to this page first, then used.

## What the Monitor Is

The Monitor describes what populist actors did around the world, month by month. It does not analyse, judge or predict. Populism is the object of study, never the target.

## What Is in an Issue

Three parts: the month in brief; around the world, in six regions; new research. An issue has 15 pages at most.

One story is one item, told as it stood at the end of the month, in 120 to 150 words. Under it stand the actor, with the dataset or the publication behind it, the sources, and a link to the research on the topic in the [Library](../library/index.qmd).

A region where nothing met the rules says so. It is never padded.

"New research" is a count, not a judgement: the works published that month that are in the Library, by their date of publication in the open catalogue OpenAlex. The full list is one click away.

## Who Is Covered {#who}

The Monitor does not decide who is populist. Research does. An actor is covered when one of these classifies it as populist:

- **[The PopuList](https://popu-list.org)**, version 4.0: parties in 31 European countries. Its borderline cases are covered too, and marked.
- **[The Global Populism Database](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/LFTQEZ)**, version 2.1: the speeches of presidents and prime ministers in 77 countries, graded from 0 to 2. A leader counts with an average of 0.5 or more in the latest term (0.5 rounds up to 1: clearly populist). The Monitor follows the leader and the party or government that the leader heads.
- **A peer-reviewed publication**, for an actor that is in no dataset. It is enough that the publication classifies the actor as partially populist. The reference is printed next to the name.

An actor is followed in or out of parliament and government. Leaders who have died, parties that no longer exist and governments that a listed actor no longer heads are not followed.

## What Counts as News {#news}

Actions, not words: elections; entering or leaving government; laws; foreign and defence policy moves; court rulings; party splits; changes of leader. No polls. No social media posts.

Any level counts: the government an actor leads, the party, its leader, a member of parliament or another representative; national, regional or local.

Left out: thin news, which no listed source reports solidly; court rulings and moves inside a party, unless they matter internationally; events that the actor did not bring about. An event abroad is filed under the actor's region.

## Sources {#sources}

The list is fixed. A source that is not on it is not used. The Monitor does not claim that its sources are neutral: nobody can prove that. It shows which sources it uses, why, and where their limits are.

### News Agencies

An agency is on the list when it has a service in English and is not owned by a state. Agencies sell their reports to media on every side of politics: they report, they do not comment.

Reuters
: Thomson Reuters; bound by its Trust Principles since 1941. All regions.

Associated Press (AP)
: A not-for-profit cooperative of news organisations in the United States. All regions.

Agence France-Presse (AFP)
: Independent by a French law of 1957. Part of its income comes from the French state, so it is never the only source on French politics. All regions.

Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa)
: About 170 German media companies. Germany.

ANSA
: A cooperative of Italian newspaper publishers. Italy.

PA Media
: A private company; most of its shareholders are British newspaper publishers. The United Kingdom and Ireland.

Press Trust of India (PTI)
: A non-profit cooperative of Indian newspapers. India.

Kyodo News
: A non-profit cooperative of Japanese newspapers and the broadcaster NHK. Japan.

Australian Associated Press (AAP)
: A not-for-profit body with no shareholders. Australia.

Two reports count as two sources only when each agency did its own reporting. A source with a link to a state is checked against the [State Media Monitor](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17219015).

### Politico Europe

For the institutions of the European Union only. It mixes news with analysis, and its owner, Axel Springer, states political values of its own. So the Monitor takes only facts from it (votes, decisions, dates) and never uses it as the only source.

### Regional Sources

For Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East and North Africa, where most agencies are run by the state. A regional source is based in the region, is not owned by a state or a party, has published standards and publishes in English. There are at most three for each region, checked every year against the trust scores of the [Digital News Report](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2026) of the Reuters Institute.

So far: News24, South Africa (Media24, part of Naspers); The Punch, Nigeria (the family of its founder); Buenos Aires Times, Argentina (Editorial Perfil).

### Official Records

Election results, court rulings, laws and the records of the European Union's institutions.

### How the Sources Are Used

- Only news reports, never opinion pieces.
- Two sources for a full item where it matters, and always for a contested fact, which is attributed.
- In the three regions above: one agency and, where one reported the event, one regional source.
- The Monitor's own words. Quotations are short.
- Every item links to its sources. The PDF prints their addresses too, because links die.
- An agency report may be read in a copy carried by another outlet, which the item names.
- A report behind a paywall is used only when the event matters and the editor has the full text.

## How an Issue Is Made {#making}

Every week the listed sources are searched for news on the listed actors, and a short note is kept for each event. The month closes on its last day. The issue is written once, in the week that follows, and comes out about a week after the month closes.

An index of events, such as Wikipedia's "Current events" pages, may help to find the reports. It is never a source.

The editor sets the rules, decides what goes into an issue and answers for every word. See the [editorial policy](../about/editorial-policy.qmd).

## Limits {#limits}

- **A Western core.** Outside Europe and the Asia-Pacific region, Reuters, AP and AFP carry most of the items.
- **English only.** Events reported only in other languages can be missed, most of all in Latin America and French-speaking Africa.
- **Small events can be missed.**
- **Selection.** About four full items for each region is a choice. The rules guide it. They do not remove it.

## Corrections and Replies

A published PDF is never changed silently. Corrections and the right of reply follow the [editorial policy](../about/editorial-policy.qmd).

## Changes to These Rules {#changes}

Version 1.4, 3 October 2026
: The page is shorter and plainer. One rule changed: for an actor that is in no dataset, a peer-reviewed publication that classifies it as partially populist is now enough. Issue 2026/1 follows version 1.3. Versions 1.0 to 1.3 are of 1 and 2 October 2026.
